young.html: Henrik Ibsen was a playwright from Norway. Before him, most serious plays were about kings, gods and heroes. Ibsen wrote about ordinary families in ordinary living rooms, and the secrets they keep.

In his most famous play, A Doll's House, a young mother named Nora seems to have a perfect, cozy life. But she has a secret: years ago, when her husband was very sick, she borrowed money in secret to save him, and she broke a rule to do it. When the secret comes out, her husband cares more about what people will think than about her. Nora realizes she has been treated like a doll, and she decides she must learn to think for herself.

young.name: gb-ibsen-past
young.cap: In each play, a secret from the past comes out. Start with A Doll's House.

young.html: For parents: these are plays for older readers. A Doll's House is the best start for teens; the other three end in tragedy, which the lesson mentions without detail.

Act it out. A play is meant to be performed. With family members, act out a short scene where one person has to tell an important truth. How does each person feel? Try it two ways: the truth told gently, and blurted out. What changes?

full.html: Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906) grew up in Skien, Norway, apprenticed to a pharmacist, and worked for years as a theater director in Bergen and Christiania (now Oslo). He then lived abroad, in Italy and Germany, from 1864 to 1891. After the great verse dramas Brand and Peer Gynt, he turned to prose plays set in middle-class homes. The Britannica set includes four: A Doll's House (1879), The Wild Duck (1884), Hedda Gabler (1890) and The Master Builder (1892). The Scottish critic William Archer translated and championed them in English.

Ibsen borrowed a technique from Greek tragedy, especially Oedipus: the most important events have already happened before the curtain rises. The play is the slow bringing to light of the past, and each revelation forces the characters to see themselves anew.

full.name: gb-ibsen-past
full.cap: Our summaries of the four plays: pick each one.

full.html: Nora Helmer seems a playful, pampered wife whom her husband Torvald calls his "little squirrel." Years ago she secretly borrowed money to save his life, forging her father's signature. When the lender, Krogstad, threatens to reveal it, Nora hopes for a "miracle": that Torvald will take the blame on himself. Instead he thinks only of his reputation. In the last scene she tells him she is leaving:

full.text:
HELMER. Before all else you are a wife and a mother.

NORA. That I no longer believe. I think that before all else I am a human being, just as much as you are—or at least I will try to become one.
full.author: Ibsen
full.ed: Ibsen's Prose Dramas, ed. William Archer (Walter Scott, London)
full.note: Archer's translation of A Doll's House first appeared in 1889.

full.html: The slam of the door as Nora leaves shocked audiences across Europe; a German actress refused to play the ending, and Ibsen reluctantly wrote an alternative for that production. The play became central to debates about marriage and women's rights. Ibsen himself said he had written about the need for every person to become themselves, more than about any political cause.
The idealist Gregers Werle insists on telling his friend Hjalmar Ekdal the truth about his family's past, sure that truth will make their marriage nobler. The doctor Relling disagrees:

full.text: Rob the average man of his life-illusion, and you rob him of his happiness at the same time.
full.author: Ibsen
full.ed: Ibsen's Prose Dramas, ed. William Archer (Walter Scott, London)

full.html: Gregers's truth breaks the family apart and ends in a heartbreaking tragedy. Readers still argue whether Ibsen is mocking his own earlier faith in truth-telling or warning about truth used without love.

full.text: Hedda Gabler and The Master Builder

full.html: Hedda Gabler is the portrait of a proud, bored woman who wants power over someone's fate and is trapped by her own choices. The Master Builder shows an aging architect, haunted by guilt over how his fortune began and afraid of the young, who climbs one last tower. Both end in tragedy.

Ibsen made the living room a place for tragedy. His characters speak everyday prose, yet each play asks a large question: what we owe ourselves, what we owe others, and when the truth heals or wounds.
Reading A Doll's House only as a pamphlet. Nora and Torvald are both people of their time; the play asks what a real marriage would require of both of them.

items: Sophocles' Oedipus, earlier on this ladder, gave Ibsen the shape of a play that uncovers the past.
Mill, in The Subjection of Women (1869), argued for women's equality in marriage; Ibsen's Nora dramatized such questions a decade later.
Kierkegaard, Ibsen's Scandinavian predecessor, also wrote about becoming oneself.
Later playwrights, from Chekhov to Arthur Miller, learned from his realism.
Is the truth always worth telling? When might it be kinder to wait, or to tell it differently?
What does it mean to become a person in your own right?
How do secrets from the past shape a family?
Why might a play about an ordinary home shock a whole continent?

questions: Nora kept a secret to protect someone. Was that right?
What do you think Nora and Torvald should have done differently?
Gregers believed everyone must know the whole truth. Do you agree?
What does it mean to think for yourself?
Why do you think Ibsen ended A Doll's House with a door closing?
